title: The work a brand sprint should leave behind
metaTitle: What a brand sprint must decide
excerpt: Leave a brand sprint with one sentence, a small palette, type, and a logo that works at a small size. Options and no decision leave the website where it started.
alt: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree. A small set of things, which is what a sprint should leave behind.
caption: A ledge with only what the room needs. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a brand sprint produce?
faqs.answer: One sentence a stranger could almost use, a small palette whose colors have jobs, type set in a real paragraph, and a logo that still reads in a browser tab. The person who can refuse the sentence later has to approve it in the room. Three directions and a plan to decide next month means the sprint did not finish.

faqs.question: How small should the palette be?
faqs.answer: Background, text, one action, and one quiet support are enough for most young brands. Name the colors by job so a button does not drift. Check that text is readable on the backgrounds you will actually use. Twelve swatches labeled flexible are how every template invents another color.

faqs.question: What should the sprint skip?
faqs.answer: Skip a long guideline nobody will open, extra slogans, and mock applications such as a bus wrap. One applied test matters: the sentence, the type, the palette, and the logo together in a rough page header. If that frame looks like two brands, the sprint is not done.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Brand sprint deliverables should be small enough to decide and sturdy enough to start a website. Leave with one sentence, a small palette, type, and a logo that works small. A sprint that ends in three options and no decision leaves the website project where it started: with taste still open and a deadline that thought identity was finished.

The sprint is a decision meeting with artifacts. It is not a presentation of possibilities for someone else to resolve later. If nobody in the room can choose, do not run the sprint yet. Run the conversation that makes a choice possible.

## The sentence

Write one sentence the company can repeat. Who it is for, and what it does, in words a stranger can use. “A shop for one clothing line, sold directly, with the cloth and the cut in the first screen.” “A product for operators who need one next action, not a tour of the data.” The sentence is not a tagline you print on a tote. It is the test for every later choice. If the palette, the type, and the homepage can all ignore it, it is not a sentence. It is a caption.

Read it aloud. If it could describe a competitor equally well, tighten it. If it depends on a word you would not say on a call, replace the word. The website will have to say this, or something that agrees with it, in the first screen. Nielsen Norman Group’s piece on [how long users stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/), from 2011, is blunt about that screen: people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and a clear value proposition in the first 10 seconds is what earns more time. The sprint sentence is the raw material for that proposition. Leaving the sprint without it means the homepage workshop will invent strategy under the guise of headlines.

Write a second line only if you need a boundary. “We do not sound breathless. We do not say we are for everyone.” Boundaries are deliverables. They stop the next round from “just trying” a voice you already refused.

Get the sentence approved by the person who can refuse it later. A sentence the founder has not heard will be relitigated on the homepage, and the sprint will have been a poster session.

## A small palette

Choose a short list of colors with jobs. Background, text, one action, one quiet support, and a line or border if you need it. Name them by the job, not only by a poetic label. “Action” is more useful than “dusk” when an engineer is styling a button months later. You can keep the poetic name in the brand note if it helps the team remember. The job is what the website will follow.

Record the values in a form the build can use, and check contrast for text on background and for the action color used as text or as a control. A palette that looks rich in a slide and fails when a sentence sits on it is not finished. The [W3C’s WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the reference for that check: text and controls have to be perceivable, not only on a moodboard in a dark room.

Do not leave with twelve swatches “to stay flexible.” Flexibility here is how every template invents a thirteenth. If you need a dark section and a light section, specify both, including the text color on each. If photography will carry the color and the UI should stay quiet, say that, and keep the UI list even shorter.

Test the palette on a sentence of real copy and on a photograph you actually have. A color that only works on the sprint’s stock image will embarrass the first real page. Wabisabi’s public site is a calm brand site. That kind of calm is a small palette used with discipline, not a large palette used shyly.

## Type that can set a page

Pick the type you will use, not a menu of type you might use. One face for headlines and one for text is enough for most young brands. Sometimes one face in a few sizes is enough. Write the sizes and the weights for the headline, the body, and the button. You are not building a full type system for a company of hundreds. You are preventing the website from becoming five fonts in five templates.

Set a real paragraph, not a single elegant word. The paragraph will show if the face is tiring, if the numerals look odd in a price, and if the bold is loud in a way the sentence of the brand refuses. Set a long product name and a short one. Set the sentence from the sprint at the size the first screen will use.

Decide the rules that stop drift. Sentence case or title case. Straight quotes. Which dashes you use. Whether you shout in caps. These are small and they are the voice. A sprint that picks a typeface and leaves the rules unsaid will be re-picked by every person who writes a button.

License the faces for the web, and put the files or the subscription in a place the build can reach. A beautiful choice nobody can ship is a concept, not a deliverable. Note the fallback if a page must render before the file loads.

## A logo that works small

The logo has to survive a browser tab, a nav bar, and a social preview, not only a title slide. Test it at the small size on both a light and a dark ground if you use both. If it falls apart, simplify it now, in the sprint, while the people who can approve the change are in the room.

Deliver the versions you will actually load. Horizontal and mark, if both are needed. SVG for the interface, and a PNG fallback if you have a real reason. Clear space as a simple rule, not as a poster. Incorrect uses can be three lines: do not recolor it ad hoc, do not stretch it, do not put it on a photograph where it disappears.

The logo is not the brand system. If the sprint spends its hours on fifty logo sketches and the last twenty minutes on the sentence, you have inverted the work. A decent mark with a true sentence will start a website. A remarkable mark with no sentence will start another round of “what are we.”

Show the mark next to the wordmark in the nav of a rough page, even a gray box page. The test is whether a stranger can find the name. Thomas Bewick’s public site is an editorial heritage project, where the name has to sit with long reading. A sports brand such as Ballarat Box Sports needs the name to sit with a louder photograph. The sprint should pick the context you actually have.

## What you may skip

Skip a forty-page guideline. Nobody will read it during the website project, and it will be wrong in places you have not built yet. A short note that holds the sentence, the palette with jobs, the type rules, and the logo files will be opened. The long book can wait until the site has taught you what the book should protect.

Skip alternate slogans. Pick none, or pick one, and treat it as copy you might use, not as a second strategy. Skip illustration systems you have no plan to draw. Skip a motion manifesto. If a single motion principle matters, one sentence is enough: “Almost nothing moves. Menus open, and the rest is still.”

Skip fake applications. A mock storefront, a mock app icon set, a bus wrap. They eat the day and they are not the website. One applied test is worth it: the homepage header, type, color, logo, and the sprint sentence set together. If that frame looks like two brands, the sprint is not done.

Skip consensus that is really postponement. “Let’s show both to the team next month” means the sprint did not decide. Either extend the room until it decides, or stop and admit the website project does not have an identity yet. Both are cleaner than a folder labeled final that contains three directions.

## Hand the result to the website

Put the files where the build will find them. Name them. Write the sentence at the top of the note so it is not buried under the logo exports. If a client portal will hold brand files after delivery, put them there too, but the project thread should have the note on day one of the site work.

The first website template should use only these decisions. When someone asks for a new color in week two, point at the palette. When they ask for a new voice, point at the sentence. The sprint failed if those requests feel reasonable because the deliverables were too vague to refuse anything.

A website project and a product project sometimes start in the same season. They should inherit the same sentence, the same type, and the same names for the same objects. [When a website project is also a product project](/blog/when-a-website-project-is-also-a-product-project) is the next piece, because a sprint that only dresses the marketing site will open a seam the moment someone logs in.

To see identity decisions carried into finished public sites, look through [Hanabi’s selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful sprint is the one you can still recognize in those pages, small and intact.
